https://telex.hu/after/2026/08/01/adela-.text: Menü Kereső Kislányként azt hitte, Hannah Montana egy szlovák szupersztár, végül maga vált azzá After frissítve Adéla Demi Lovato It's Not That Deep turnéján 2026. május 16-án – Fotó: Maya Dehlin Spach/Getty Images for ABA Bányász Dorka A 22 évesen Adéla Jergová a kétezres évek Lady Gagájától megszokott grandiózus koncepciókkal, tökéletesre csiszolt tánctudással és a sötét, érzelmes témákat boncolgató elektropop zenéjével jó úton halad, hogy a következő generáció popikonja legyen. Az augusztustól első önálló turnéjára induló szlovák énekesnő művészi identitása azonban nem egyik napról a másikra született meg, de mindig is kristálytiszta célok vezérelték. Az énekesnő július végén megjelent kislemeze, az Ain't in LA csak egy ízelítő a szeptemberben érkező Prima nevet viselő nagylemezéből. Az Ain't in LA és maga Adéla is bebizonyítja, hogy nem elérhetetlen cél az amerikai álom, a menő lányokat pedig nem Los Angelesben kell keresni, hanem akár kelet-európai városokban is. Ilyen az, amikor valaki sztárnak születik Adéla, aki Pozsonyban született, már egészen korán tudta, hogy sztár szeretne lenni. Csakúgy, mint sok más kortársa, ő is Hannah Montana szoknyája mögül bújt ki . Több interjúban is felelevenítette egyik gyermekkori élményét, amikor a sorozat szlovák szinkronos változatát nézte, és Hannah Montanáról azt gondolta, hogy egy szlovák szupersztár. Amikor a bátyja elmondta, hogy Miley Cyrus valójában amerikai, azonnal beindult a fantáziája, és elkezdett angolul tanulni úgy, hogy Demi Lovato és Cyrus interjúit nézte. Adéla saját bevallása szerint egy éven belül folyékonyan és akcentus nélkül beszélt angolul, és már akkor pontosan tudta, hogyan képzeli el a jövőjét. Kikereste a Disney Channel címét és felírta egy papírra afféle manifesztációként: 15 éves korára Los Angelesbe fog utazni. A terve nem jött be, nem jutott el a Disneyhez (talán jobb is), helyette teljesen elmerült a balett világában. A balett kifinomult művészeti vonala közelebb állt a sok hozzá hasonló, kelet-európai lányhoz, és a szülei is inkább ebbe az irányba próbálták terelni. A művészeti pályája akkor fordult komolyra, amikor 14 évesen elköltözött otthonról, hogy hivatásos balerina lehessen, tini kora nagy részét egyedül, Bécsben, majd Londonban töltötte. Az énekesnő elmondása szerint ez az időszak nem volt könnyű számára, és a Hannah Montana ihlette sztárkarrier lehetősége még mindig ott lebegett a szeme előtt. Végül 18 évesen az Egyesült Államokban kötött ki, hogy részt vegyen a Pop Star Academy című műsorban, amiben a Hybe és a Geffen Records a Katseye nevű globális lányegyüttes tagjait kereste. Bár versenytársai körében az egyik legnagyobb esélyesnek számított, viszonylag korán kiesett, de ez sem szegte a kedvét. Az itt szerzett tapasztalatai és a balett világa ébresztette rá, hogy teljesen mást akar kezdeni magával. Megijesztette az elvárás, hogy mindig szépen mosolyogjon, makulátlan legyen a kinézete, és hogy állandóan a tökéletesség sugározzon róla. „Össze voltam zavarodva. Miért vagyok itt, ha úgyis mindenről mások fognak dönteni? Nekem szükségem van arra, hogy egy kicsit csúnya és furcsa lehessek, nem akarom, hogy az a nyomás nehezedjen rám, hogy állandóan szép és tökéletes legyek” – mesélte Adéla egy interjúban. A legjobb dolog, hogy kiesett Az addig szőke, bájos énekesnő élete teljes fordulatot vett a Pop Star Academy után. Ekkor jött a vibráló pink haj, a füstös smink, a piros talpú Christian Louboutin tűsarkú és a szakadt neccharisnya, amikkel mind a 2010-es évek pop időszakát elevenítette fel. Az énekesnő tavaly megjelent első EP-je, a The Provocateur (ahogy a címe is sejteti) provokatív, nyers és koszos hangzású elektropop esztétikával robbant be, a producerek között pedig olyan zenészek is feltűntek, mint 100 gecs duóból ismert Dylan Brady, Grimes vagy a Troye Sivan Rush számáért felelős Alex Chapman. Adéla rendetlen imázsát tetőzte még az EP-hez készült borító is, amin az énekesnő látszólag egy falat vizel le, ezzel megidézve Sophy Rickett 1990-es Pissing Women fotósorozatát , ami szintén megosztó volt a megjelenésekor. A megosztó lét nem ijeszti meg az énekesnőt, sőt, egyenesen élvezi, ha megbotránkoznak rajta, és ez más zenészeknek is feltűnt. Az EP első száma, a Superscar felkeltette Grimes érdeklődését , aki végül Machine Girl zenéjének videoklipjében is feltűnt, Adélát pedig a jövő popsztárjának nevezte. Később a SexOnTheBeat számának videoklipjében Christina Aguilera is szerepelt. A The Provocateur esztétikájához sokat adott az énekesnő megjelenése is, ami pont Aguilera stylistjának, Chris Horannek köszönhető, aki a tavalyi Szigeten is fellépő Charli XCX öltözködéséért is felelős. Horan egyébként maga kereste fel az énekesnőt, még akkor, amikor csak pár száma jelent meg, ketten pedig megalkották azt az avantgárd, szakadt balerina kinézetet, ami mostanra Adéla védjegye lett. „Egy pillanatra arra gondoltam, miért áll ki mellettem mindenki, aki menő? Elfogott az imposztor-szindróma” – mondta az énekesnő a Rolling Stone magazinnak . A sztárságig vezető lázálom pedig nem áll meg itt. Az énekesnő első EP-je után Troye Sivan, Rachel Sennott, Demi Lovato és még sokan mások árasztották el Adélát dicséretekkel. Lovato fel is kérte az énekesnőt, hogy turnézzon vele, Adéla pedig eleget téve a felkérésnek fekete tüllszoknyából kibukkanó, neonpink tangában és balettcipőben nyitotta Lovato turnéállomásait. Az előadást Robbie Blue koreografálta, aki olyan nevekkel dolgozott már együtt, mint Tate McRae, Doechii, Lady Gaga vagy FKA twigs. A pop prímabalerinája Az énekesnő szeptemberben érkező nagylemeze, a Prima kettős jelentéssel bír. A balettben nevelkedő Adéla lemezének címe egyszerre utal a debütálására, egyben a balett társulatok vezető táncosának, a prímabalerinának a rangjára is. „A pop prímabalerinája akarok lenni, és ez az első lépésem ennek eléréséhez” – mondta Jergová. Az énekesnő lemezén visszatérő producer lesz Dylan Brady és Blake Slatkin, aki nemrég Sienna Spiro The Visitor című debütáló lemezén, korábban pedig Gracie Abrams This Is What It Feels Like és minor című lemezein is dolgozott. A céltudatos énekesnő Owen Thiele műsorában olyan popdívákat nevezett meg inspirációnak, mint Britney Spears, Ariana Grande, Janet Jackson vagy Beyoncé, akiknek imázsa, hangja és perszónája kikerülhetetlen. Az időnként kirívó és megbotránkoztató fellépései és videóklipjei ellenére sikerült megőriznie a gyökereit. Adéla gyerekkora óta a popsztár életről álmodott, és a színpadon érzi magát igazán önmagának. A karrierjébe tett energia megtérülni látszik, az énekesnő előtt pedig egyértelműen nagy jövő áll. Adéla jelenleg azon előadók táborát erősíti, akikre érdemes odafigyelni, hiszen autentikusan önmagát adja, és nem görcsöl rá a dolgokra: „A nap végén én csak egy pop lány vagyok. Fiatal vagyok, énekelni és táncolni szeretnék. És nagyon őszinte akarok lenni. Ezek jelenleg a sarkcsillagaim, aztán meglátjuk, hogy alakulnak a dolgok.” Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! http://www.heraldglobe.com/news/27930556.text: NATO scrambles jet over flock of birds RT.com 14 Sep 2026, 18:01 GMT+10 The mistaken drone sighting caused the closure of Vilnius airport, the Lithuanian authorities have said A NATO fighter jet took flight after a flock of birds was confused with drones, the Lithuanian authorities have reported. There have been a number of incidents of Ukrainian UAVs crossing the airspace of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia or crashing in those countries as Kiev has intensified its long-range attacks on energy infrastructure in Leningrad Region in northwestern Russia in recent months. On Sunday, a perceived drone sighting caused the closure of Vilnius International Airport, the country's National Crisis Management Center said in a statement later that day. It was reopened within 40 minutes after a NATO jet, which had taken off from Siauliai airbase in the north of the country, found that the cause of the air alert was not a UAV, but a flock of birds, it said. "On initial radar readings, marks left by birds and drones can be similar," the statement read. The Siauliai airbase hosts Italian air force Eurofighter Typhoon aircraft, which had been deployed to Lithuania as part of the NATO Baltic Air Policing mission. Flying a Eurofighter Typhoon jet for a single hour reportedly costs around $65,000. Last month, NATO said that its warplanes shot down a drone over Latvia, claiming that it entered the Baltic nation's airspace "as a result of Russian electronic warfare activities." Russia has accused Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia of playing with fire by allowing their territory to be used for hostile activity. Russian officials have warned that if the Baltic nations knowingly help facilitate Ukrainian drone strikes, Moscow would consider them complicit in the attacks and would have the right to self-defense under the UN Charter. The false alarm in Lithuania comes amid growing speculation about incidents involving alleged Russian drones across Europe. In July, the International Institute of Strategic Studies (IISS) said that surveillance UAVs had been spotted on 144 occasions near key infrastructure facilities, airports and airbases in UK, France, Belgium and the Netherlands and other countries. However, none of the aircraft were ever captured, with Russian denying any involvement. Earlier this month, the German government claimed it had grounds to believe that Russia was behind an incident in which an explosive-laden UAV was found between Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4. Berlin hasn't provided any proof linking the drone to Moscow. Russian President Vladimir Putin denied the German accusations, saying that they were being used to distract the public from domestic economic woes. Moscow has said repeatedly that it harbors no aggressive designs against Europe, adding that a conflict with NATO is only possible if the Western bloc attacks Russia first or if its members deploy their forces to Ukraine. http://www.editorandpublisher.com/storie.text: Your reporting is solid. Can you afford to defend it? Facing a lawsuit seeking more than €400,000, Delfi turned to Reporters Shield for help funding its defense. Investigative editor Holger Roonemaa explains what that support means for the journalism still to come. LEARN MORE ABOUT REPORTERS SHIELD The story was published. Then came a demand for more than €400,000—and a lawsuit naming the reporter personally alongside the news organization that published his work. For Holger Roonemaa, head of the investigative and fact-checking desk at Delfi Estonia, the experience illustrates how quickly the cost of investigative journalism can extend far beyond the reporting budget. A newsroom can stand behind its work and still face an expensive fight to defend it. Delfi was already a member of Reporters Shield , a nonprofit membership organization that helps newsrooms defend public interest journalism against legal threats, when the lawsuit arrived. Roonemaa says that membership gave the newsroom financial support at a moment when defending the investigation threatened to consume resources needed for the next one. “They covered all of our legal fees to defend ourselves,” he said. An investigation into money and political influence The reporting examined an Estonian banker and businessman’s influence within the conservative Isamaa party, where he was a major donor, according to Roonemaa. The public interest question was how financial power translated into influence over a political organization. Roonemaa said a reporter on his team requested access to files from a criminal investigation involving the businessman, who had been acquitted. Within those files, the reporter found emails and transcripts of intercepted calls that, Roonemaa said, shed light on the businessman’s involvement in internal party affairs. The resulting story focused on that political influence. According to Roonemaa, the businessman then sued over the publication of his personal data, sought more than €400,000 in damages and demanded removal of numerous passages, including some that did not identify him by name. The claim targeted both Delfi and the individual reporter. That personal exposure is especially troubling to Roonemaa, who emphasizes that publication follows an editorial process rather than a reporter acting alone. The cost begins before the verdict The financial demand was only one source of pressure. Roonemaa describes the hours, days and sometimes weeks required to organize evidence, prepare materials for court and work with lawyers. Those responsibilities fall on journalists who would otherwise be pursuing their next investigation. Even a newsroom confident in its reporting must devote time to defending work it has already completed. “We don’t want to spend time on something that we have already done,” he said. Reporters Shield cannot give those hours back. Nor, Roonemaa explains, does the support he describes eliminate the possibility of damages if the newsroom ultimately loses. The uncertainty remains, particularly for a reporter named personally in the proceedings. What changes is the concern about paying for the legal defense. Roonemaa says cases like this can generate legal fees running into tens of thousands of euros. Having those fees covered allows the publisher to preserve money for reporting while contesting the claim. “We know that we will have the best possible defense and then representation,” he said. “And that gives a really big level of assurance to you.” A first court victory with an appeal still pending At the time of the interview, Roonemaa said Delfi had prevailed in the first court instance and the investigation remained online. He described the ruling as strongly supportive of the newsroom and said the judge characterized the action as a SLAPP—a strategic lawsuit against public participation. That characterization mattered to the team. Roonemaa said the decision also attracted coverage from other Estonian news organizations, bringing wider attention to the dispute and its implications for journalism. The case, however, was under appeal. Roonemaa was clear that the first decision could still be upheld or reversed. The newsroom’s experience demonstrates the value of support during a continuing legal battle, with the final outcome still uncertain. Good reporting still needs a defense Roonemaa sees a difficult paradox in investigative journalism: in his experience, some of the strongest, most carefully checked stories can provoke the strongest resistance. Thorough editing and fact-checking do not prevent someone from filing a lawsuit. That does not diminish the newsroom’s responsibility to get the work right. He describes rigorous reporting standards as central to Delfi’s relationship with Reporters Shield, including careful editing, fact-checking and, in some cases, legal review before publication. For Roonemaa, membership reinforces the need to put the full effort into each investigation. Support for the defense works alongside that discipline, giving editors greater assurance when well-supported reporting is challenged. Keeping the next investigation possible The value extends beyond the journalists handling the case. Roonemaa says having support for legal costs gives his company’s leadership more confidence about continuing to invest in investigative reporting. That investment already requires salaries and substantial reporting time. Litigation can multiply the expense and complicate decisions about what the newsroom can afford to take on next. For Delfi, Reporters Shield’s support helps protect the resources behind those decisions. The published investigation remains available while the legal process continues, and the newsroom can keep pursuing further reporting without carrying the same burden of defense costs. The next important story will still require evidence, careful editing and an editor willing to publish. Roonemaa’s experience shows why publishers also need to consider how they will pay to defend that decision. About Reporters Shield: Reporters Shield is an independent, nonprofit membership organization that defends investigative and public-interest journalism from legal threats designed to silence critical reporting. Through members’ contributions to a mutual defense fund and donations from donors, the organization covers its members’ legal costs. Serving print, digital, and nonprofit newsrooms globally, the organization provides legal support and resources to help journalists publish with confidence. It was developed by investigative journalists and media lawyers, with support from leading legal institutions and funders committed to defending press freedom. For more information, contact info@reporters-shield.org . Manage Preferences Estonia already recognises the concept of professional confidentiality and members of certain professions have the right to refuse to testify. However, Justice Minister Liisa Pakosta (Eesti 200) says the relevant provisions in existing legislation are too narrow and unclear. "Our idea is to establish clear professional privileges. This is different from professional confidentiality. Professional privilege specifically means that people working in certain professions who may come into possession of information that could, for example, be relevant to a criminal investigation are not required, and in some cases are not permitted, to disclose that information to investigative authorities," Pakosta explained. Such clearly defined professional privileges could apply to lawyers, notaries, victim support workers, bankruptcy trustees, clergy, journalists and patent attorneys. Estonian Bar Association President Imbi Jürgen said such violations of privacy in criminal proceedings are not merely a theoretical threat. "The biggest concern at present is the interception of calls between lawyers and their clients during surveillance operations. This is a very serious problem and disputes concerning the issue have also reached the Supreme Court," Jürgen said. Justice Minister Pakosta acknowledged that protecting members of these professions would also make certain crimes more difficult to investigate. "If the state wants to convict someone, it must gather all the evidence itself. It cannot assume that just because someone has told their story to a journalist, that means they can be convicted on that basis the following day," Pakosta said. Chief State Prosecutor Taavi Pern said the Prosecutor's Office welcomes the proposal, as the law governing these professions has so far been relatively unclear. "Both the Bar Association and the Prosecutor's Office have been telling the Ministry of Justice for years that this bill and more precise regulations are needed," Pern said. According to Pern, the bill will increase the Prosecutor's Office's workload. "If we have to carry out various investigative procedures involving people covered by professional privilege, such as conducting searches or arguing in court over whether the contents of certain emails are protected by professional confidentiality, this will add to our workload," Pern said. Despite the additional workload, the state does not plan to allocate any extra funding to the Prosecutor's Office. This could mean that prosecutors will have to reorganize their work. "Given how complex criminal proceedings have become, it would be welcome if discussions about any legislative amendments also included consideration of how many resources, for example, the Prosecutor's Office or the courts would need to implement them," Pern said. Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Pictures of damaged houses have attracted hundreds of comments on social media. Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty Images UK news Criminals recruiting children to damage Greater Manchester HMOs, police believe Houses being targeted because they are thought to hold immigrants, with dozens of properties affected in recent weeks Hannah Al-Othman North of England correspondent Fri 23 Oct 2026 14.19 EDT Last modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 14.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Criminals are recruiting vulnerable people, including children, to damage houses suspected of being HMOs, police in Manchester believe. In recent weeks, dozens of properties have been targeted across Greater Manchester, mostly in Salford, but also in Stockport and Tameside. The houses that have been attacked are either HMOs (houses in multiple occupation), or properties that have been mistaken for HMOs. Police have received at least 46 separate reports of criminal damage, with cars also targeted alongside houses. Windows have been smashed, and walls and doors have been sprayed with graffiti reading “fuck off” and “no HMO”. Houses are being targeted because they are believed to hold immigrants or refugees. Ch Supt Marcus Noden said: “We suspect vulnerable people are being exploited and paid to damage buildings they believe are HMOs. Some of those being exploited are believed to be children.” “This recent spate of damage is not being tolerated,” he added. “A 42-year-old man has today been arrested on suspicion of causing criminal damage at an address in Salford overnight. He remains in our custody for questioning.” Previously Noden said that officers were “taking this spate of damage extremely seriously and are continuing to relentlessly target offenders, including those who we believe are using and exploiting children to orchestrate the criminality”. Salford council has also taken down roadside banners that had been put up, which read: “IRLAM AND CADISHEAD SAY NO TO MIGRANT HMOs.” In a statement, the council said: “We have serious concerns that the impact of the banners is highly likely to spread misinformation, escalate cohesion issues in communities and the potential for inciteful behaviour.” Police have also said that social media is fuelling the attacks, which began on 5 October, with online platforms being used to “push the message out across different areas”. Posts with pictures of the damaged houses have attracted hundreds of comments, many of them praising the attacks and predicting further violence. However, some have also been critical of the criminal campaign of damage, including domestic abuse survivors who had recently been housed in HMOs. Four people have been arrested this week in relation to the attacks. On Monday, a 46-year-old man and a 39-year-old man were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage, and on Wednesday a 33-year-old man was also arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage. Police have also made previous arrests in relation to the spate of criminal damage, including a 13-year-old boy.
